summary.text: For odd \(p\), set \(T=2(p-1)\) and split the defining sum at \(T\): every term in the initial block contains either \(2^{p-1}-1\) or \(2^T-1\), hence vanishes modulo \(p\), while Fermat’s theorem together with \(\binom{T+k+1}{2}\equiv\binom{k+1}{2}\pmod{p-1}\) makes the shifted block agree termwise with the original sum. For \(p=2\), the recurrence \(a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\) shows inductively that every \(a(n)\) with \(n\ge1\) is odd.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),
\]
where an empty product is understood to be \(1\). Since
\(\binom{k+1}{2}=k(k+1)/2\), this is exactly the sequence in the statement.
We prove that for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq 1\),
\[
 a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]

We first record a recurrence that will handle the prime \(2\). Splitting the defining sum for \(a(n+1)\) into the terms with \(0\leq k<n\) and the final term \(k=n\), we obtain
\[
 a(n+1)=(2^n-1)a(n)+2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for each \(k<n\), the product occurring in the corresponding summand of \(a(n+1)\) is
\[
 \prod_{j=k+1}^{n}(2^j-1)
 =(2^n-1)\prod_{j=k+1}^{n-1}(2^j-1),
\]
so the sum of all these terms is \((2^n-1)a(n)\). For \(k=n\), the product is empty and hence equals \(1\), leaving the final term \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\).

It follows from (1) that
\[
 a(n)\equiv 1\pmod 2 \qquad(n\geq 1). \tag{2}
\]
The base case is \(a(1)=1\). If \(n\geq1\) and \(a(n)\) is odd, then \(2^n-1\) is odd, while \(\binom{n+1}{2}\geq1\), so \(2^{\binom{n+1}{2}}\) is even. Thus (1) says that \(a(n+1)\) is odd, proving (2) by induction.

Now let \(p\) be prime and let \(n\geq1\).

If \(p=2\), then \(2(p-1)=2\). By (2), both \(a(n+2)\) and \(a(n)\) are congruent to \(1\) modulo \(2\). Hence the desired congruence holds in this case.

It remains to consider an odd prime \(p\). Put
\[
 T=2(p-1).
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), and Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
 2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{3}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 2^T=2^{2(p-1)}=(2^{p-1})^2\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{4}
\]
Equivalently, both \(2^{p-1}-1\) and \(2^T-1\) are divisible by \(p\).

We split the defining sum for \(a(n+T)\) at \(k=T\). Writing the indices in the second part as \(k=T+r\), this gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 a(n+T)
={}&\sum_{k=0}^{T-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)\\
 &+\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{T+r+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=T+r+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1). \tag{5}
\end{aligned}
\]
We will show that the first sum vanishes modulo \(p\), and that the second sum is congruent to \(a(n)\).

Consider first a summand in the first sum, so that \(0\leq k<T\). There are two cases.

If \(k+1\leq p-1\), then the index \(j=p-1\) lies in the interval from \(k+1\) to \(T+n-1\). Indeed, the lower-bound condition is our assumption, and the upper-bound condition follows from \(T=2(p-1)\) and \(n\geq1\). Therefore the product in this summand contains the factor
\[
 2^{p-1}-1,
\]
which is divisible by \(p\) by (3).

If instead \(k+1>p-1\), then the index \(j=T\) lies in the same interval. The lower bound holds because \(k<T\), hence \(k+1\leq T\), and the upper bound holds because \(n\geq1\), hence \(T\leq T+n-1\). Thus the product contains the factor
\[
 2^T-1,
\]
which is divisible by \(p\) by (4).

In either case the product, and hence the entire summand, is divisible by \(p\). It follows that
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{T-1}2^{\binom{k+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=k+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 \equiv0\pmod p. \tag{6}
\]

We next compare the second sum in (5) with the defining sum for \(a(n)\). Two periodicity observations are needed.

First, for every nonnegative integer \(j\), (4) implies
\[
 2^{T+j}=2^T2^j\equiv2^j\pmod p. \tag{7}
\]
Thus shifting an exponent of \(2\) by \(T\) does not change its residue modulo \(p\).

Second, the triangular-number exponent in the coefficient also has the required periodicity. For every \(r\geq0\), direct algebra gives the exact integer identity
\[
 \binom{T+r+1}{2}
 =\binom{r+1}{2}+(p-1)(2r+2p-1). \tag{8}
\]
To see this, use \(T=2(p-1)\) and compute
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \binom{T+r+1}{2}-\binom{r+1}{2}
 &=\frac{(T+r+1)(T+r)-r(r+1)}2\\
 &=\frac{T(2r+T+1)}2\\
 &=(p-1)\bigl(2r+2(p-1)+1\bigr)\\
 &=(p-1)(2r+2p-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the difference between the two exponents in (8) is a multiple of \(p-1\). By (3), or equivalently by repeatedly removing factors \(2^{p-1}\), we get
\[
 2^{\binom{T+r+1}{2}}
 \equiv 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}\pmod p. \tag{9}
\]

Now fix \(r\) with \(0\leq r<n\). Reindex the product in its summand of the second sum in (5) by writing \(j=T+i\). As \(j\) runs from \(T+r+1\) through \(T+n-1\), the new index \(i\) runs from \(r+1\) through \(n-1\). Hence
\[
 \prod_{j=T+r+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 =\prod_{i=r+1}^{n-1}(2^{T+i}-1).
\]
By (7), each factor on the right satisfies
\[
 2^{T+i}-1\equiv2^i-1\pmod p,
\]
and therefore
\[
 \prod_{j=T+r+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 \equiv\prod_{i=r+1}^{n-1}(2^i-1)\pmod p. \tag{10}
\]
This remains valid when the products are empty.

Combining (9) and (10), the \(r\)-th summand in the second sum of (5) is congruent modulo \(p\) to
\[
 2^{\binom{r+1}{2}}
 \prod_{i=r+1}^{n-1}(2^i-1),
\]
which is precisely the \(r\)-th summand in the definition of \(a(n)\). Summing over \(0\leq r<n\), we conclude that
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{n-1}2^{\binom{T+r+1}{2}}
       \prod_{j=T+r+1}^{T+n-1}(2^j-1)
 \equiv a(n)\pmod p. \tag{11}
\]

Finally, substitute (6) and (11) into the decomposition (5). The first part contributes \(0\) modulo \(p\), and the second contributes \(a(n)\). Thus
\[
 a(n+T)\equiv a(n)\pmod p.
\]
Since \(T=2(p-1)\), this is exactly
\[
 \boxed{a\bigl(n+2(p-1)\bigr)\equiv a(n)\pmod p}
\]
for every prime \(p\) and every \(n\geq1\), as required.
